items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think I worked with Stan first and then Bill... I did that one recording with Bill. “Live at Montreux.”

ctx.x: We're in 66' at this point if you're just forming Charles Lloyd...

Well yeah, he came later. That was my first band that toured internationally. We started touring Europe, and George was getting gigs on the fly as we were going over there and getting a lot of press. He knew how to bill the band. We were constantly going to Europe and then coming back, then going out to the West coast. That group subsequently got invited in ‘67… …we got invited to play in Russia and we got invited there, no fee, no money, but George saw this as great exposure, for the band to get international…

we got there they had to hide us. There was a knock on the door and they were asking "Was anybody there?" and they said "No no, there's nobody there," and we don't know what happened to this guy after we left, but George capitalized on it and we got a lot of press from that. . . When we came back, the Dreamweaver album apparently sold over a million copies, which for that time was really good. The Charles Lloyd Quartet was bridging that crossover stuff that was happening, and then we played gigs opposite Miles…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom

ctx.x: I heard you probably in around 1968 or so, with Charles Lloyd. And I’d had a couple of — I’ll call them epiphanies now but that was another one. This was in Rochester in some hall, and I think it was the first time I’d heard drummers and bassists really — I’ll call it playing with the time. Not straight ahead but a little bit of elastic approach to the time.

Well the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom for each individual to be playing collectively but have an equal input. And so after that “Live at the Village Vanguard” you know it kind of just spread throughout the jazz community. So you know you could break time up. Break it up. And then go into the time later. But for coloring it really opened that up.

Is it possible to feel the time — I’m thinking of Latin music with the clave that is almost always there but sometimes no one’s playing it. So I guess I’m trying to relate that to a jazz situation where everybody’s feeling it but — I can’t quite finish this question but it’s an interesting thing to observe and hear when the time is there but no one is enforcing it regularly.
